extra.message: The SignUpForm exposes the `role` field with `choices=User.ROLE_CHOICES` which includes `school_admin`, `instructor`, `teaching_assistant`, and `student`. A user registering an account can set their role to any of these values, including `school_admin`. This allows a standard user to create an account with full administrative privileges without any authorization check. The `initial='student'` only sets the default value in the UI but does not prevent the user from changing it to a privileged role via form submission.

The SignUpForm exposes the `role` field directly to users during self-registration. The field includes all possible role choices including `school_admin`, allowing any user to sign up as a school administrator, instructor, or teaching assistant — bypassing all role-based access controls.

In GradeForm.clean_points(), the upper-bound check (`points > max_points`) is only performed when `self.instance` exists. The condition `max_points = self.instance.submission.assignment.max_points if self.instance else None` means that if the form is ever used without a pre-existing GradeRecord instance (new grade creation), `max_points` is None and the upper-bound validation is entirely skipped. This could allow a grader to set points higher than the assignment's max_points on first grading.

The WebhookForm allows users to configure any URL for the webhook endpoint via the `url` field (a URLField). There is no validation restricting URLs to public/external destinations. If the webhook delivery mechanism makes HTTP requests to these URLs (which is the intended behavior), a malicious user could configure a webhook pointing to internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254/`), internal admin panels, or other private network services, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). The `url = models.URLField()` in the model also does not restrict the destination.

The Submission model's FileField uses a hardcoded `FileExtensionValidator` with `allowed_extensions=["pdf", "docx", "txt", "zip", "py", "ipynb", "xlsx"]`. The Assignment model has an `allowed_file_types` field (line 186-190) intended for instructors to restrict accepted file types per assignment. However, the model-level validation and SubmissionForm validation both hardcode their own accept-list of extensions rather than using `assignment.allowed_extensions_list()`. This means an instructor who configures an assignment to only accept `pdf` files cannot actually enforce this — students can still upload `py`, `zip`, `ipynb`, or `xlsx` files because the model validator permits them.

The ApiKey model stores the 'key' field as a plain CharField(max_length=64, unique=True) without hashing. API keys function as authentication credentials equivalent to passwords. They should be hashed (like passwords) after generation, with the raw key shown only once at creation time. Storing them in plaintext means any database compromise leaks all API keys permanently.

The Webhook model stores the 'secret' field as a plain CharField(max_length=64) without any encryption or hashing. If an attacker gains database access (SQL injection, backup exposure, DB admin compromise), all webhook secrets are immediately readable in plaintext. These secrets authenticate webhook payloads and could be used to forge webhook requests to external systems or verify forged callbacks.

The API key value is rendered directly in the HTML template as {{ k.key }}. This exposes the full API key to any user who can view the API keys page. API keys are sensitive credentials that should not be fully displayed after initial creation.

The API keys template renders the full API key in the HTML for every page load via {{ k.key }}. This exposes the credential in the page source, browser history, proxy logs, and any screenshots/shared screens. API keys should only be shown once at creation time.

The notification link (`{{ n.link }}`) is rendered directly in an `href` attribute without URL scheme validation. Django's auto-escaping only encodes HTML special characters (`<`, `>`, `"`, `&`, `'`), but does not sanitize or validate URL protocols. An attacker who can control the `link` field of a Notification can inject a `javascript:` URL (e.g., `javascript:alert(document.cookie)`). When a user clicks the link, the browser decodes the HTML entities and executes the JavaScript. The Notification model's `link` field is a plain CharField with no URL validation, providing no protection at the data layer.

The notification link (`{{ n.link }}`) is rendered directly in an `href` attribute on the student dashboard without URL scheme validation. Django's auto-escaping only encodes HTML special characters but does not sanitize URL protocols. An attacker who can control the `link` field of a Notification can inject a `javascript:` URL (e.g., `javascript:alert(document.cookie)`). When a student user clicks the link, the browser executes the JavaScript. This is the same vulnerability pattern as notifications.html but in a separate template file serving a different user context.

The webhook secret value is rendered directly in the HTML template as {{ h.secret }}. This exposes the full webhook secret to any user who can view the webhooks page. Webhook secrets are sensitive credentials used to sign webhook payloads.

The webhooks template renders the webhook secret in plaintext via {{ h.secret }} for every page load. The secret is displayed in the HTML source, visible in browser cache, proxy logs, and shared screens. Webhook secrets authenticate payloads and should be masked after creation.

The login endpoint at `/accounts/login/` uses Django's built-in `auth_views.LoginView` with no rate limiting, account lockout, failed-attempt counter, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff. This allows an attacker to perform unlimited brute-force password guessing attacks against any user account. Django's LoginView does not include any built-in rate limiting mechanisms — it must be added via middleware like django-axes, django-ratelimit, or custom decorators.

The password reset confirmation endpoint at `/accounts/reset/<uidb64>/<token>/` uses Django's built-in `auth_views.PasswordResetConfirmView` with no rate limiting. While the token provides some protection, an attacker could attempt to brute-force the reset token or repeatedly submit invalid tokens without restriction.
The `get_client_ip` function trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header without validation, allowing an attacker to spoof their IP address by sending a crafted header.

The `course_catalog` view returns ALL courses without filtering by status by default. While it accepts a `status` filter parameter, it does not enforce showing only active courses to unauthenticated users.

The public course_catalog endpoint (no login required) executes Course.objects.all() without any default status filtering. Courses in 'draft', 'archived', or other non-public statuses are exposed to any visitor. The home endpoint (line 58) correctly filters by status='active', but the catalog does not.
The signup endpoint has no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff. An attacker can create thousands of accounts programmatically without restriction.
The change_password endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker who compromises a session or CSRF token could rapidly change a user's password without restriction.
The audit log view allows school admins to search logs by description content using query parameter `q`. Audit log descriptions may contain sensitive user information.
The CSV import handler opens uploaded files without validating file size, content type, or MIME type, making it vulnerable to resource exhaustion via large file uploads or upload of non-CSV files.

The CSV user import allows the `role` field to be set directly from the CSV row data. A user who can upload a CSV can create accounts with elevated privileges (e.g., school_admin) by specifying `role=school_admin` in the CSV.

The admin_import CSV import function creates users with passwords read directly from the CSV file, defaulting to 'changeme123' if no password column is provided. There is no validation of password strength or enforcement of the application's password policy (min 8 chars, complexity requirements) during bulk import.
The CSV bulk user import accepts and sets passwords from CSV file data with a weak default of 'changeme123', creating user accounts with weak or blank passwords.

The CSV user import function defaults the password to 'changeme123' if the CSV row does not contain a password field. This means all imported users without an explicit password will share the same weak, predictable password.

Student display names, assignment titles, and feedback fields are written to CSV without sanitizing cells that start with formula characters (=, +, -, @). When opened in spreadsheet applications (Excel, Sheets), these can execute arbitrary formulas.

Course titles, cohort names, assignment titles, student names, and other user-controlled fields are written to CSV without sanitizing formula characters. This is a second instance of CWE-1236 at a different export endpoint.

The file upload endpoint accepts any file type without validating the content type, file extension, or scanning the file content. An attacker can upload malicious files (e.g., executable scripts, HTML with JavaScript).

In `file_download`, if a Resource has no associated course (`resource.course` is None), the authorization check is skipped entirely, allowing any authenticated user to download any resource by ID regardless of ownership.
Webhook secrets are generated using `uuid.uuid4().hex` which uses a random UUID. While not cryptographically broken, UUID4 is not a CSPRNG-based token generator as recommended for security secrets.

User-uploaded file's name (drop_blob.name) is passed directly to FileSystemStorage.save() without sanitization. A malicious filename containing '../' sequences can write files outside the intended 'incoming' directory.

User-controlled GET parameter 'packet_ref' is passed to FileSystemStorage.save() without sanitization. A malicious packet_ref value containing '../' sequences can write files outside the intended directory.

The `course_grade_file_096` endpoint has no authentication or authorization check. Unlike all other course operations functions in this file, it does NOT call `_wrk_gate(request)` to verify the internal operations token. This endpoint is publicly accessible without any authentication.

The course_return_lane_163 endpoint redirects users to a URL controlled via GET/POST parameter without any validation. The 'lane' parameter can be any path or full URL, enabling an open redirect vulnerability.
The `lane` parameter from user-controlled GET or POST data is used directly as a redirect target with no validation, creating an open redirect vulnerability.
Untrusted data from the HTTP request body or GET parameter is directly deserialized using pickle.loads(). Deserializing untrusted pickle data leads to arbitrary code execution.

User-controlled request body or GET parameter 'blob' is passed directly to pickle.loads() for deserialization. Pickle is inherently unsafe and can execute arbitrary Python code during deserialization.
The `pickle.loads()` function is called on raw user-supplied data from the request body or GET parameter. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data leads to arbitrary code execution.
Arbitrary JSON from the request body is merged into the workset dictionary without validation, allowing an attacker to set sensitive fields like 'role', 'tier', 'approved', and 'balance'.

User-controlled JSON payload from the request body is merged directly into a workset dictionary via `workset.update(payload)`. The workset contains privileged fields (`role`, `approved`, `balance`, `tier`) that the user can overwrite.

User-controlled GET parameter 'ref' is used to construct a file path without any sanitization. The ref value is formatted as '{ref}.json' and joined with BASE_EXPORT_DIR, allowing directory traversal with '../' sequences. Additionally, sensitive data (SSN, credit card numbers) is written to the traversed path.
Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers from GET parameters are written to disk in cleartext as JSON files, exposing sensitive PII and financial data.

Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are passed as GET query parameters. Query parameters are logged by web servers, proxies, and browser history, permanently storing this sensitive PII in log files.
SSN (social security number) and credit card numbers are accepted as GET parameters and written to a JSON file on disk in cleartext. This violates PCI DSS and data protection regulations.

The `course_crumb_lane_300` function sets a `portal_crumb` cookie without `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, or `SameSite` attributes. The cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP and is accessible to JavaScript, making it susceptible to interception and XSS attacks.
The cookie `portal_crumb` is set without `httponly`, `secure`, or `samesite` flags, making it accessible to JavaScript and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP.

The `course_identity_ping_344` endpoint has no authentication or authorization check. Unlike other course operations functions, it does NOT call `_wrk_gate(request)`. This endpoint accepts user handles and channels without any authentication.
Hardcoded verifier values '4812' and '5930' for handles 'north' and 'south' are embedded in the source code as authentication credentials.

The Origin request header is reflected as the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true, allowing any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.

The course_origin_mirror_661 endpoint reflects the Origin request header as the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true. This allows any cross-origin website to make authenticated requests with the user's credentials.
The `Origin` request header is reflected as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, allowing any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.

The X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly set to 0 (disabling XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is set to empty string (disabling CSP), making the application more vulnerable to XSS and clickjacking attacks.
The endpoint explicitly disables the X-XSS-Protection header (set to '0') and sets an empty Content-Security-Policy. This weakens browser security protections for responses from this endpoint.
The X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly set to 0 (disabling browser XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is set to empty string (disabling CSP), removing critical browser security protections.

User-controlled input from the 'fragment' GET parameter is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This enables Server-Side Template Injection leading to Remote Code Execution.

User-controlled `fragment` parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows arbitrary Jinja2 template expression execution, which can lead to remote code execution.
User-controlled `fragment` GET parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows arbitrary server-side template injection that can lead to RCE.

The course_jinja_cast_683 endpoint renders a Jinja2 template containing a user-controlled fragment from the GET parameter 'fragment'. Jinja2 templates can execute arbitrary Python expressions (e.g., {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[2].__subclasses__() }}) leading to RCE. Additionally, complex templates or infinite loops can cause denial of service.
User-controlled input is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), which can lead to remote code execution in Jinja2.

The `course_badge_gate_691` function makes an authorization decision (granting elevated access to 'payroll' and 'casework' data) based on the `ops_badge` cookie value. Cookies are entirely client-controlled — any attacker can set `Cookie: ops_badge=lead` to bypass access controls.

User-controlled `host` parameter from GET request is concatenated directly into a shell command via os.system(). No sanitization or escaping is performed on the host input before passing it to the OS shell.

The course_shell_probe_701 endpoint runs `os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host)` where `host` is taken directly from the `host` GET parameter without sanitization. An attacker can specify internal IP addresses (e.g., 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254) to probe internal network services, or use shell metacharacters for command injection.

The MongoDB connection string defaults to `mongodb://localhost:27017` without any authentication if the MONGO_URL environment variable is not set. This allows unauthenticated access to the MongoDB instance. Even if MONGO_URL is set, if it doesn't include credentials, access is unauthenticated.

User-controlled JSON payload is parsed and passed directly as a MongoDB filter query to find_one(). An attacker can inject NoSQL query operators ($ne, $regex, $gt, etc.) to manipulate the query logic.
User-supplied JSON body is parsed and used directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like $ne, $regex, $where to manipulate queries.
The MongoDB connection URL from environment does not include TLS/SSL parameters. When connecting to MongoDB over a network, the connection may not be encrypted or verified, exposing data in transit.

The course_mongo_lane_711 endpoint accepts a user-controlled MongoDB filter from the request body and executes it without any query limits or restrictions. An attacker can send expensive, unbounded queries that can exhaust database resources.
User-controlled JSON payload is used directly as a MongoDB query filter. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like `$ne`, `$regex`, `$where` to bypass authentication or extract data.
SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using `ssl._create_unverified_context()`, making HTTPS requests vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle attacks.

The endpoint makes an HTTP request to a hardcoded external URL with SSL verification disabled. Though the URL is hardcoded, combined with the disabled verification, an attacker could potentially redirect the connection.

The XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False, enabling external entity resolution. Untrusted XML from request body is parsed with this dangerous configuration.

The course_xml_fold_735 endpoint parses XML with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, and `no_network=False`, enabling XML External Entity (XXE) attacks. An attacker can send a crafted XML payload to: (1) cause denial of service via billion laughs entity expansion, (2) read local files via external entities, (3) perform SSRF to internal services.
The XML parser is configured with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, and `no_network=False`, allowing external entity resolution from user-supplied XML, enabling XXE attacks.
The endpoint exposes internal server configuration including the Django settings module name and base export directory path in the response.

The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'django-insecure-local-dev-only' when the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. This known value can be used to forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and any data signed by Django's signing framework.
A fallback SECRET_KEY 'django-insecure-local-dev-only' is hardcoded in settings.py. If SECRET_KEY is not set in the environment, Django will use this weak, publicly known key.
The DATABASE_URL contains embedded credentials (`lms_user:lms_pass`) in plaintext in the code. Even if overridden by environment, the fallback value exposes database credentials.

The database connection string contains hardcoded credentials (`lms_user:lms_pass`) as the default fallback. These plaintext credentials are embedded directly in the source code and would be used if the DATABASE_URL environment variable is not set.

The database password falls back to the hardcoded value 'lms_pass' when the DATABASE_URL environment variable is not set or does not contain a password. This is a second instance of hardcoded credentials.
